DiagProgMeta

Meta-analysis of diagnostic and prognostic studies: SROC curves and sensitivity analysis for publication bias

DiagProgMeta is an R package for the meta-analysis of

  • diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) studies: the summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curve and the area under the SROC curve (SAUC) by the bivariate random-effects model (Reitsma et al., 2005), and
  • prognostic studies: the time-dependent SROC curve and SAUC, where the time-dependent sensitivity and specificity are reconstructed from the published survival probabilities (Hattori and Zhou, 2016),

each with a likelihood-based sensitivity analysis for publication bias (Zhou et al., 2023).

Without publication bias Sensitivity analysis for publication bias
Diagnostic studies (SROC) reitsma.sroc() srocsa.t()
Prognostic studies (time-dependent SROC) hattori.tsroc() tsrocsa.lrt()

All four fitting functions come with print(), summary(), and plot() methods.

The repository is named srocsa, but the package name is DiagProgMeta.

Installation

The development version can be installed from GitHub:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("kusuri26/srocsa")

Alternatively,

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("kusuri26/srocsa")

DiagProgMeta requires R (>= 3.5) and imports lifecycle, mixmeta, and numDeriv.

library(DiagProgMeta)

Example 1: diagnostic studies (SROC curve)

The IVD data (Safdar et al., 2005) contain the 2 x 2 tables (TP, FN, FP, TN) of 33 diagnostic studies.

data(IVD)
head(IVD)
#>   study TP FN  FP  TN cutoff.grp type cutoff
#> 1     1 12  0  29 289          1   SQ     15
#> 2     2 10  2  14  72          2   SQ   1000
#> 3     3 17  1  36  85          1   SQ     15
#> 4     4 13  0  18  67          2   SQ   1000
#> 5     5  4  0  21 225          1   SQ     15
#> 6     6 15  2 122 403          1   SQ     15

Without publication bias: reitsma.sroc() 

fit.sroc <- reitsma.sroc(TP = TP, FN = FN, FP = FP, TN = TN, data = IVD)
print(fit.sroc)
#> SROC curve: bivariate random-effects model (Reitsma et al., 2005)
#> Publication bias is not considered
#> 
#>   K Conv  SAUC         95% CI  Sens         95% CI  Spec         95% CI
#>  33  yes 0.874 [0.806, 0.920] 0.815 [0.757, 0.862] 0.861 [0.821, 0.893]
#> 
#> Estimates (tau1, tau2: between-study SDs; rho: correlation):
#>    mu1   mu2  tau1  tau2    rho
#>  1.484 1.824 0.597 0.826 -0.424

summary() adds the standard errors and confidence intervals of all the parameters and the summary sensitivity, specificity, and SAUC.

summary(fit.sroc)
#> SROC curve: bivariate random-effects model (Reitsma et al., 2005)
#> Publication bias is not considered
#> 
#> Call:
#> reitsma.sroc(TP = TP, FN = FN, FP = FP, TN = TN, data = IVD)
#> 
#> ============================================================
#> Results
#> ============================================================
#> Number of studies: 33
#> Convergence:       yes (relative convergence (4))
#> Log-likelihood:    -31.076
#> 
#> Parameters (tau1, tau2: between-study SDs; rho: correlation)
#> ------------------------------------------------------------
#>      Estimate    SE          95% CI
#> mu1     1.484 0.177  [1.136, 1.832]
#> mu2     1.824 0.154  [1.522, 2.125]
#> tau1    0.597 0.175  [0.336, 1.062]
#> tau2    0.826 0.117  [0.626, 1.090]
#> rho    -0.424 0.236 [-0.769, 0.111]
#> 
#> Summary measures
#> ------------------------------------------------------------
#>             Estimate         95% CI
#> Sensitivity    0.815 [0.757, 0.862]
#> Specificity    0.861 [0.821, 0.893]
#> SAUC           0.874 [0.806, 0.920]
#> 
#> All estimates (par.all)
#> ------------------------------------------------------------
#>    mu1    mu2 tau1^2 tau2^2  tau12   sauc   sens   spec 
#>  1.484  1.824  0.357  0.683 -0.209  0.874  0.815  0.861

The SROC curve with its pointwise confidence band, the summary point with its confidence region, and the studies (point size proportional to the precision):

plot(fit.sroc, plot.ci = TRUE, spoint.region = TRUE,
     add.study = TRUE, study.size = "precision")

Sensitivity analysis for publication bias: srocsa.t()

The model is fitted for each marginal selection probability pp in sa.p. p=1p = 1 corresponds to no publication bias; a smaller pp assumes that a smaller proportion of the studies is published.

fit.sa <- srocsa.t(TP = TP, FN = FN, TN = TN, FP = FP, data = IVD, sa.p = c(1, 0.8, 0.6))
print(fit.sa)
#> ==================================================
#> Model optimization
#> 
#> Number of studies : 33 
#> Optimizer         : 1 1 1 
#> 
#> * 1 indicates converged
#> ==================================================
#> 
#> SAUC Estimates
#> -------------------------------------------
#> Marginal p    SAUC      SE   CI.low   CI.up
#> -------------------------------------------
#> p = 1        0.874   0.029    0.806   0.920
#> p = 0.8      0.871   0.030    0.800   0.919
#> p = 0.6      0.822   0.041    0.727   0.889
#> 
#> ==================================================
#> 
#> Parameter Estimates (SE)
#> -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> Marginal p           mu_se           mu_sp          tau_se          tau_sp              rho            beta         alpha
#> -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> p = 1        1.484 (0.177)   1.824 (0.154)   0.597 (0.175)   0.826 (0.117)   -0.424 (0.236)               -             -
#> p = 0.8      1.472 (0.177)   1.818 (0.154)   0.607 (0.179)   0.828 (0.118)   -0.404 (0.241)   5.000 (5.396)    -7.943 (-)
#> p = 0.6      1.234 (0.150)   1.681 (0.153)   0.618 (0.202)   0.850 (0.127)   -0.275 (0.270)   5.000 (4.126)   -10.451 (-)
## tables of the SAUC and the parameter estimates
res <- summary(fit.sa)

res$sauc

## SROC curves and summary points for each p, with the studies
plot(fit.sa, sroc.cols = c("black", "blue", "red"), add.study = TRUE)

The change of the SROC curve and SAUC as pp decreases shows the potential impact of publication bias.

Example 2: prognostic studies (time-dependent SROC curve)

The Ki67 data are a list of three data frames:

Element Content Columns used below
Ki67$OS Survival probabilities of the test-positive (1) and test-negative (0) groups, one row for each study and each time point study, t, n1, n0, s1, s0
Ki67$HR Hazard ratio (group 1 vs 0) and its 95% CI, one row for each study study, HR, ci.low, ci.up
Ki67$MT Survival probabilities at the median follow-up time, used to estimate the censoring distribution mct_mo, n1, n0, s1_mct, s0_mct 
data(Ki67)
Ki67_OS <- Ki67$OS
Ki67_HR <- Ki67$HR
Ki67_MT <- Ki67$MT

## lnHR and its variance from the HR and its 95% CI
Ki67_HR$lnHR     <- log(Ki67_HR$HR)
Ki67_HR$lnHR.var <- ((log(Ki67_HR$ci.up) - log(Ki67_HR$ci.low)) / (2 * qnorm(0.975)))^2

Without publication bias: hattori.tsroc()

The bivariate random-effects model is fitted at each time point in time.points.

fit.tsroc <- hattori.tsroc(
  time.points = c(24, 36, 60),
  study.os = study, time.os = t, n1.os = n1, n0.os = n0, s1.os = s1, s0.os = s0,
  data.os = Ki67_OS,
  study.lnhr = study, lnhr = lnHR, var.lnHR = lnHR.var,
  data.lnhr = Ki67_HR,
  time.med = mct_mo, n1.med = n1, n0.med = n0, s1.med = s1_mct, s0.med = s0_mct,
  data.mt = Ki67_MT
)

## one row for each time point
print(fit.tsroc)
#> Time-dependent SROC curve: bivariate random-effects model at each time point
#> (Hattori and Zhou, 2016); publication bias is not considered
#> 
#>         K Conv  SAUC         95% CI  Sens         95% CI  Spec         95% CI
#> t = 24 23  yes 0.713 [0.628, 0.785] 0.743 [0.647, 0.821] 0.562 [0.506, 0.617]
#> t = 36 23  yes 0.651 [0.610, 0.690] 0.662 [0.577, 0.738] 0.570 [0.515, 0.624]
#> t = 60 21  yes 0.647 [0.610, 0.682] 0.630 [0.567, 0.688] 0.587 [0.522, 0.649]
#> 
#> Estimates (tau1, tau2: between-study SDs; rho: correlation):
#>          mu1   mu2  tau1  tau2    rho
#> t = 24 1.063 0.249 0.911 0.520 -0.515
#> t = 36 0.673 0.284 0.656 0.512 -0.877
#> t = 60 0.532 0.353 0.430 0.577 -0.928
## estimates with SEs and confidence intervals at each time point
summary(fit.tsroc)

By default, plot() draws one plot for each time point; in an interactive session, press Return to move to the next time point. A single time point can be selected by time, and all the time points can be overlaid in one panel by overlay = TRUE.

plot(fit.tsroc)                              # one plot per time point
plot(fit.tsroc, time = 36, add.study = TRUE) # one time point with the studies
plot(fit.tsroc, overlay = TRUE)              # all the time points in one panel

Sensitivity analysis for publication bias: tsrocsa.lrt()

The selection function is on the tt-statistic of lnHR. The model is fitted for each time point in time.points and each pp in senp.p.

fit.tsa <- tsrocsa.lrt(
  time.points = c(36, 60),
  study.os = study, time.os = t, n1.os = n1, n0.os = n0, s1.os = s1, s0.os = s0,
  data.os = Ki67_OS,
  study.lnhr = study, lnhr = lnHR, var.lnHR = lnHR.var,
  data.lnhr = Ki67_HR,
  time.med = mct_mo, n1.med = n1, n0.med = n0, s1.med = s1_mct, s0.med = s0_mct,
  data.mt = Ki67_MT,
  senp.p = c(1, 0.8)
)
print(fit.tsa)

One plot for each time point (curves for each pp), or all in one panel (color: time point, line type: pp):

plot(fit.tsa, time = 60, add.study = TRUE)

Methods

SROC curve (reitsma.sroc)

Let y1iy_{1i} and y2iy_{2i} be the logit-transformed sensitivity and specificity of study ii, and v1iv_{1i} and v2iv_{2i} be their variances. The bivariate random-effects model (Reitsma et al., 2005) is

(y1i,y2i)⊤∼N((μ1,μ2)⊤,diag(v1i,v2i)+Ω), (y_{1i}, y_{2i})^\top \sim N\left((\mu_1, \mu_2)^\top,\ \mathrm{diag}(v_{1i}, v_{2i}) + \Omega\right),

where Ω\Omega has the between-study standard deviations τ1,τ2\tau_1, \tau_2 and correlation ρ\rho. The SROC curve is

logit(TPR)=μ1−τ1ρτ2{logit(FPR)+μ2}, \mathrm{logit}(\mathrm{TPR}) = \mu_1 - \frac{\tau_1 \rho}{\tau_2}\left\{\mathrm{logit}(\mathrm{FPR}) + \mu_2\right\},

and the SAUC is the area under it. The confidence interval of the SAUC is calculated by the delta method on the logit scale.

Sensitivity analysis on the SROC curve (srocsa.t)

The probability of publishing study ii is modeled by the selection function Φ(α+βti)\Phi(\alpha + \beta t_i) with

ti=c1y1i+c2y2ic12v1i+c22v2i,c1,c2≥0,c12+c22=1. t_i = \frac{c_1 y_{1i} + c_2 y_{2i}}{\sqrt{c_1^2 v_{1i} + c_2^2 v_{2i}}}, \quad c_1, c_2 \ge 0, \quad c_1^2 + c_2^2 = 1.

For a given marginal selection probability pp, α\alpha is determined such that the mean of the inverse of the marginal selection probabilities of the observed studies equals 1/p1/p. The model is fitted by the maximum likelihood method for each pp in sa.p. c12c_1^2 is estimated by default, or fixed by the argument c11.

Time-dependent SROC curve (hattori.tsroc)

At each time point tt, the time-dependent sensitivity and specificity are reconstructed from the survival probabilities S1(t)S_1(t) and S0(t)S_0(t) of the test-positive and test-negative groups (Combescure et al., 2016):

Se(t)={1−S1(t)}q1{1−S1(t)}q1+{1−S0(t)}q0,Sp(t)=S0(t)q0S1(t)q1+S0(t)q0, \mathrm{Se}(t) = \frac{\{1 - S_1(t)\} q_1}{\{1 - S_1(t)\} q_1 + \{1 - S_0(t)\} q_0}, \qquad \mathrm{Sp}(t) = \frac{S_0(t) q_0}{S_1(t) q_1 + S_0(t) q_0},

where q1q_1 and q0q_0 are the proportions of the two groups. Their within-study variances and covariance are calculated from the survival probabilities up to tt, assuming a censoring distribution common to all the studies, estimated from the median follow-up time. The bivariate random-effects model (with the within-study covariance) is fitted at each time point (Hattori and Zhou, 2016).

Sensitivity analysis on the time-dependent SROC curve (tsrocsa.lrt)

The logit-transformed sensitivity, specificity, and the log hazard ratio (lnHR) are modeled by the trivariate random-effects model, combined with the selection function on the tt-statistic of lnHR. The time-dependent SROC curve and SAUC are calculated from the parameters of the logit-transformed sensitivity and specificity.

Three data frames are required by hattori.tsroc() and tsrocsa.lrt():

Argument Content
data.os Survival probabilities of the two groups, one row for each study and each time point (sorted by time within each study)
data.lnhr lnHR and its variance, one row for each study
data.mt Survival probabilities at the median follow-up time, used to estimate the censoring distribution

See ?tsrocsa.lrt for the details of each column.

Functions

Function Description
reitsma.sroc() Bivariate random-effects model for the SROC curve and SAUC, without publication bias
srocsa.t() Sensitivity analysis for publication bias on the SROC curve and SAUC
hattori.tsroc() Time-dependent SROC curve and SAUC, without publication bias
tsrocsa.lrt() Sensitivity analysis for publication bias on the time-dependent SROC curve and SAUC
sauc() SAUC and its confidence interval (delta method on the logit scale)

Methods

Method "sroc" objects (reitsma.sroc(), hattori.tsroc()) "srocsa" objects (srocsa.t(), tsrocsa.lrt())
print() Number of studies, convergence, SAUC, sensitivity, specificity (with CIs), and the parameter estimates; one row for each time point SAUC and parameter estimates for each pp (and each time point)
summary() Estimates, SEs, and CIs of (μ1,μ2,τ1,τ2,ρ)(\mu_1, \mu_2, \tau_1, \tau_2, \rho), log-likelihood, and all estimates Tables of the SAUC ($sauc) and the parameter estimates ($coef)
plot() SROC curve(s); options time, overlay, plot.ci, spoint.region, add.study SROC curves for each pp; options time, p, overlay, plot.ci, spoint.region, add.study

Data

Data Description
IVD Meta-analysis of the diagnosis of intravascular device-related bloodstream infection (33 studies)
CD64 Meta-analysis of neutrophil CD64 for the diagnosis of bacterial infection (27 studies)
IVD_2, CD64_2 Logit-transformed sensitivity and specificity of IVD and CD64, with their variances
Ki67 Meta-analysis of Ki67 as a prognostic marker: a list of the survival data (OS), hazard ratios (HR), and median follow-up times (MT)
